title: Plaquette: A hardware-aware design platform for fault-tolerant quantum computers
authors: Raul Conchello Vendrell, Carlos Díaz López, Ish Dhand, Kshitij Kapoor, Davide Laureti, Marcello Massaro, Pranjal Nayak, Ivan Ogloblin, Martin B. Plenio, Shreya Prasanna Kumar, Matteo Santandrea, Varun Seshadri, Antal Száva, Trevor Vincent, Raphael Weber
abstract: Hardware teams building fault-tolerant quantum computers (FTQCs) must decide which imperfections to suppress, and that decision requires the logical performance of the architecture under the device's actual noise. Hardware noise often departs from the stochastic Pauli models used by scalable stabilizer simulators: superconducting transmons leak out of the computational subspace, neutral atoms scatter through intermediate states, trapped ions heat as their motional modes absorb phonons, and miscalibrated controls over-rotate coherently. We present Plaquette, a theoretical framework and software suite that computes the logical performance of fault-tolerant architectures directly from the physics of such imperfections. In Plaquette, a hardware error model is specified once, as Kraus operators, Hamiltonian-Lindblad dynamics, or an experimentally reconstructed quantum channel, and is compiled automatically into the exact or approximate representation required by each of four sampler classes: stabilizer sampling for Pauli noise, the new XPauli sampler for leakage and environment sectors, near-Clifford samplers for coherent errors, and full-state simulation for exact reference calculations. We validate the XPauli and near-Clifford samplers against full-state simulation, which they can match within statistical uncertainty while Pauli twirling can fall short depending on the error model. We demonstrate the framework on three error models: leakage in superconducting qubits, intermediate-state scattering in neutral atoms, and heating in trapped ions. The size of the discrepancy between Plaquette and Clifford-only simulations varies with platform and noise process, so reliable thresholds, error budgets, and overhead estimates require the most accurate simulation available. Plaquette provides a direct path from the open-system physics of a device to the logical performance of the FTQC built on it.
summary: The paper presents Plaquette, a novel software framework that allows researchers to calculate the true logical performance of fault-tolerant quantum computers directly from detailed physical noise models. By accepting general quantum channels derived from hardware imperfections (like leakage or heating), it moves beyond simplified Pauli approximations. This provides essential guidance for setting realistic error budgets and designing viable FTQC architectures.
main_problem: The core problem is determining the true logical performance of Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computers (FTQCs) when subjected to realistic, complex hardware noise that deviates from simple Pauli models.
main_result: The authors introduce Plaquette, a framework that provides a direct path from specifying open-system physics (as quantum channels) to calculating the logical error rates of an FTQC built on it.
method: Plaquette accepts hardware noise models specified as Kraus operators or Lindblad dynamics and compiles them for various samplers: stabilizer sampling, XPauli sampler, near-Clifford samplers, and full-state simulation.
model_or_system: The framework is designed to model physical imperfections across multiple platforms, including leakage in superconducting transmons, intermediate-state scattering in neutral atoms, and heating in trapped ions. The noise is generally modeled using CPTP quantum channels.
key_observables: Logical error rates, threshold surfaces, error budgets, and overhead estimates for fault tolerance.
important_parameters: The vector of physical parameters ($\eta$) defining the hardware noise (e.g., decay rates, detunings).
main_assumptions: The framework highlights that relying only on Clifford-only simulations can lead to overly optimistic and inaccurate estimates compared to full channel analysis.
figures_summary: Figure 1 summarizes the Plaquette workflow: specifying device physics as a channel, compiling it for sampling, and outputting logical error rates. Table I details Plaquette's capabilities across codes, error models, and platforms.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the limitations of current noise models, introduces the Plaquette framework to accept general quantum channels, validates specialized samplers (XPauli, near-Clifford) against full simulation, and demonstrates its utility on three distinct physical hardware platforms.
why_interesting: This is highly relevant as it bridges the gap between abstract QEC theory and messy, real-world open quantum system physics encountered in AMO/quantum optics experiments.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Plaquette at a glance. A QEC code defines a noiseless circuit for extracting syndrome information; an er- ror model, specified once as CPTP channels, is compiled into a noisy circuit in the exact or approximate representation that the chosen sampler requires. This noisy circuit is sam- pled and decoded; the logical performance is returned as logical error rates, which are then aggregated into thresholds, sensitivities for different error sources, and physical-logical overheads.

FIG. 2. Schematic of the Plaquette simulation workflow. A noiseless circuit is generated from a code. The noisy circuit is compiled from the noiseless circuit and the error model in the representation required by the chosen sampler. In parallel, a decoder model is compiled from the noiseless circuit and a Pauli-twirled version of the error model; the decoders included in Plaquette are initialized from the resulting detector error model. Sampling the noisy circuit produces syndromes, which are passed to the decoder; the decoder, in turn, yields the logical failure probability.

FIG. 3. State representation underlying the XPauli sampler. Each qubit carries an extended label rather than a bare two- level state. (i) Qubits in the computational subspace spanned by |0⟩and |1⟩(green) keep full coherence and are stored jointly as one stabilizer state; their level label reads comp, short for ‘computational’. (ii) A qubit in a leaked level (red) is instead tracked by a classical level label xi ∈{2, 3, . . . }. (iii) A separate sector label σi (blue) records the classical state of the qubit’s environment.
